rows.title: Body Rust: Floors, Rockers & Door Posts Rot From the Drip Rails Down
rows.howToFix: Don't chase patches. Restorers cut back to clean metal and weld in reproduction direct-fit panels (floor pans, full inner/outer rockers, door-post repair sections, kick panels), or fit a complete media-blasted and e-coated reproduction tub on rough trucks. The bulletproofing step most owners skip is corrosion PREVENTION so it never comes back: epoxy-prime all hidden/backside metal, seam-seal every welded joint, and inject cavity wax into the rockers, posts and boxed rails. Re-seal the drip rails (the original water path) and keep tailgate/cowl drains clear. Recurrence comes from inadequate protection, not the repair method itself.

rows.title: Frame Rot & Cracks at the Rear Shock Mounts and Spring Hangers

The proven bulletproofing move is to box and reinforce the high-stress areas (rear shackle mounts, shock towers) and then internally coat the rails with cavity wax/internal frame coating so the closed sections stop rusting from within. Inspect and re-weld any front-shock-tower cracks on lifted/trail trucks.

rows.title: Inadequate Front Drum Brakes (Pre-1976)
rows.howToFix: A front drum-to-disc conversion is one of the most universal Early Bronco upgrades. Bolt-on kits fit both the early Dana 30 (66-70) and Dana 44 (71-75) six-bolt knuckles with new spindles/calipers/rotors, and crucially the conversion also moves you to a dual-reservoir (split-circuit) master cylinder plus an adjustable proportioning valve, so a single line failure no longer kills all four brakes. Period-correct builders replicate it with factory 78-79 Bronco / 73-79 F-150 knuckles, spindles, calipers and backing plates; restomod builders use a complete LEED/Wild Horses kit. The result is modern, fade-free, wet-weather stopping that actually matches bigger tires.

rows.title: 6V Generator & Points Ignition — Weak, Outdated Charging/Spark
rows.howToFix: Convert to a 12-volt, negative-ground alternator and modern ignition — the single highest-value reliability upgrade on these trucks. Pull the generator and voltage regulator, fit a one-wire (or three-wire) alternator wired through a fused output to the solenoid battery stud, and either use an internally-resisted coil or add a ballast resistor. Then drop a hidden electronic-ignition module (e.g. Pertronix Ignitor) into the stock distributor for a hot, maintenance-free spark — no more points to set. Swap the bulbs, gauges/sender, coil, and starter components to 12V as needed. The payoff is bright lights, easy hot-starting, headroom for an electric fan and accessories, and no roadside points/condenser failures.

rows.title: Cab Corner, Floor Pan & Rocker Rust (Structural Body Corrosion)
rows.howToFix: Cut out the rot and weld in correct reproduction steel rather than skim-filling. Quality weld-in cab corners, full floor-pan halves with the support braces, and inner+outer rocker sets are reproduced for these trucks (CJ Pony Parts, Mill Supply, Classic Industries); replace the rockers as complete units and the cab corners as patch sections, butt-welded and metal-finished. The restorer's bulletproofing step is corrosion-proofing the repair: epoxy-prime bare metal, weld-through primer on mating flanges, then flood every box section and the inside of the rockers/cab corners with cavity wax and apply seam sealer so the new steel doesn't rot from the inside like the original did. Refresh the cab-mount bushings and re-establish factory door gaps as you go.

rows.title: In-Cab Gas Tank Behind the Seat (Fire/Fume Safety Hazard)
rows.howToFix: Restorers either restore the in-cab tank correctly or relocate it out of the cab for safety. The bulletproofing move many choose is a bed-fill or under-bed relocation kit (CJ Pony Parts, Performance Online) that moves the tank behind the rear axle under the bed, gets the fuel and fumes out of the cab, increases capacity, and is the right time to add a modern in-tank pump if going EFI. Either way, replace all rubber with ethanol-rated hose and a quality filter.

rows.title: Ethanol-Era Vapor Lock & Carburetor Fuel Boil
rows.howToFix: Bulletproof the fuel delivery against ethanol and heat. Run larger 3/8 in. ethanol-rated line routed away from the exhaust and heat-shielded/insulated where it must pass close, add a phenolic/insulating spacer under the carburetor to block manifold heat soak, and rebuild the carb with modern ethanol-resistant components (or fit a new aluminum carb). Many restorers add a return-line regulator so fuel circulates and stays cool rather than sitting and boiling, and some convert to a low-pressure electric pump near the tank to push (not pull) cool fuel forward. Use non-ethanol fuel and a stabilizer when storing. The combination ends hot-soak vapor lock and ethanol-driven leaks for good.

rows.title: Weak 4-Wheel Drum Brakes — Fade and Single-Circuit Risk

Bolt-on front drum-to-disc kits (Master Power Brakes, CPP, Wilwood, Classic Industries) add vented rotors, calipers, and the correct spindles, and crucially include a dual (split-circuit) master cylinder, a vacuum or hydroboost booster, and a proportioning valve. That gives fade-free stopping, retained braking after water, and a redundant second circuit so a single failure no longer means no brakes. Most kits install in a weekend with hand tools. Keep good drums in back or add a rear disc kit on a heavily driven restomod; either way the dual master cylinder is the non-negotiable safety upgrade.

rows.title: Y-Block Top-End Oiling Starvation (Sludged Rocker Oil Passages)

Modern detergent oil plus this combination ends the chronic top-end starvation for good.

rows.title: Twin I-Beam Kingpin & Front-End Wear (Wandering, Vague Steering)
